**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

### Initial parallel searches

1. Tavily general search, maximum five results, for:
   - “Conti ransomware as a service official indictment complaint sanctions advisory internal chats leak organizational structure aliases defendants”
   - “site:justice.gov Conti ransomware indictment defendant alias TrickBot Ryuk Conti”
   - “Conti leaks internal chats organization roles affiliates payment negotiation primary source analysis”

2. Tavily search, maximum five results, for:
   - “site:justice.gov/usao Conti Galochkin Rudenskiy Tsarev Zhuykov Lytvynenko press release aliases”
   - “site:justice.gov Conti ransomware ‘Wizard Spider’ indictment aliases defendants”
   - “site:home.treasury.gov Conti sanctions aliases Wizard Spider TrickBot”
   - “FBI CISA Conti advisory ransomware as a service affiliates operators aliases”

### Returned benchmark sources

The searches returned the same four benchmark sources. The follow-up searches did not return additional official records, sanctions, warrants, indictment text, complaint text, or specific alias-to-defendant mappings.

---

# Fully Comprehensive Findings

## 1. Source inventory and source type

### SRC-001 — Rewards for Justice, official U.S. government profile

The Rewards for Justice page is an official website of the United States Government. It offers “a reward of up to $10 million” for information leading to the identification or location of any person who, “while acting at the direction or under the control of a foreign government,” participates in malicious cyber activities against U.S. critical infrastructure in violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA). [1][SRC-001]

The page identifies malicious cyber actors known by the online aliases “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis,” and states that they “are believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group.” [1][SRC-001]

The page states that “Conti (also known as Wizard Spider), is a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group that has targeted U.S. and Western critical infrastructure.” [1][SRC-001]

The page lists the associated location as Russia; the online aliases as “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”; the associated cyberthreat organization as “Conti” and “Wizard Spider”; and the associated malicious cyber applications as “Conti ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS),” “TrickBot,” “IcedID,” “Cobalt Strike,” and “ZLoader.” [1][SRC-001]

This is an official government attribution and reward notice. It does not identify any of the five aliases as a particular named defendant in the DOJ case page described below. [1][SRC-001] [4][SRC-004]

### SRC-002 — Rapid7 analysis of leaked Conti chats

Rapid7 published “Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict.” The article is dated March 1, 2022, and was last updated May 9, 2024. It is a threat-research and analytical account of publicly released Conti chat logs and related material. [2][SRC-002]

Rapid7 reported that, on February 27, Twitter user “@ContiLeaks” released “a trove of chat logs from the ransomware group, Conti,” described as “a sophisticated ransomware group whose manual was publicly leaked last year.” [2][SRC-002]

Rapid7 stated that the information was necessarily incomplete because some messages were encrypted and could not be read. [2][SRC-002]

Rapid7 also stated that it had not accessed data requiring access to remote servers or the use of usernames and passwords, and “strongly recommend[ed] against doing so.” [2][SRC-002]

### SRC-003 — Center for Internet Security analytical account of the Conti leaks

The Center for Internet Security article, “The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization,” is an analytical account of ransomware commercialization, the RaaS model, and organizational information derived from Conti leaks. [3][SRC-003]

The article refers to reporting and analysis by other sources, including KrebsonSecurity, Bleeping Computer, Bleeping Computer’s ransom-note template, Alan Liska’s *Ransomware: Understand. Prevent. Recover.*, and an MS-ISAC perspective. Those underlying sources were referenced in the CIS article but were not separately returned as benchmark sources in the tool results. [3][SRC-003]

### SRC-004 — U.S. Department of Justice case page

The U.S. Department of Justice, Middle District of Tennessee, maintains an official case page titled “Conti Ransomware.” The page lists:

- Case number 3:23-CR-00092:
  - Maksim Galochkin
  - Maksim Rudenskiy
  - Mikhail Tsarev
  - Andrey Zhuykov
- Case number 3:23-CR-00088:
  - Oleksii Lytvynenko [4][SRC-004]

The DOJ page states that Conti ransomware “was a malicious software that affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world.” [4][SRC-004]

The page states that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. [4][SRC-004]

The DOJ page is an official record of charges and a later guilty plea by Oleksii Lytvynenko. The returned excerpt does not include the underlying indictment, complaint, warrant, or the linked press-release text. [4][SRC-004]

---

## 2. How the sources describe Conti as a ransomware-as-a-service operation

### Official Rewards for Justice description

Rewards for Justice describes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as “a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group” targeting U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. [1][SRC-001]

The page states that Conti was “first detected in 2019.” [1][SRC-001]

It states that Conti ransomware had been used to conduct “more than 1,000 ransomware operations” targeting U.S. and international critical infrastructure. The listed targets include:

- Law enforcement agencies
- Emergency medical services
- 9-1-1 dispatch centers
- Municipalities [1][SRC-001]

The page states that healthcare and first-responder networks were among “more than 400 organizations worldwide victimized by Conti,” with “over 290” located in the United States. [1][SRC-001]

Rewards for Justice describes the operational model as follows:

- Conti operators “typically steal victims’ files.”
- They encrypt servers and workstations “in an effort to force a ransom payment from the victim.”
- The ransom letter instructs victims to contact the actors through an online portal to complete the transaction.
- If the ransom is not paid, the stolen data is sold or published to a public site controlled by Conti actors.
- Ransom amounts vary widely, with some ransom demands reaching “as high as $25 million.” [1][SRC-001]

The page also states that, after Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti ransomware operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical-infrastructure organizations in countries perceived to be carrying out cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. [1][SRC-001]

### CIS description of the RaaS model

The CIS article describes the shift toward RaaS as “likely the most significant trend” in the commercialization of cybercrime. [3][SRC-003]

It states that RaaS involves groups leasing malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits with the developers, “often in a 70-30 split.” [3][SRC-003]

The article also describes initial access brokers, or IABs, as part of the RaaS relationship and states that a graphic in the article depicts “the RaaS relationship and the part that initial access brokers (IABs) play in greater detail.” [3][SRC-003]

The CIS article describes Conti as “a notorious RaaS operation that used double extortion to pressure victims into paying up.” [3][SRC-003]

The article states that Conti “also appears to have had ties to other malware outfits, most notably TrickBot.” [3][SRC-003]

The distinction between official and analytical descriptions is material:

- Rewards for Justice officially characterizes Conti as a Russian government-linked RaaS group and describes its alleged activities and targets. [1][SRC-001]
- CIS presents the RaaS model as an analytical description involving malware developers, affiliates, profit-sharing, and initial-access brokers. [3][SRC-003]
- The CIS article’s statement that Conti “appears to have had ties” to TrickBot is an analytical assessment, not a finding tied in the returned material to a particular defendant. [3][SRC-003]

---

## 3. Leak-derived organizational and operational structure

## 3.1 Provenance and scope of the leaks

Rapid7 reported that, on February 27, 2022, Twitter user “@ContiLeaks” released a large collection of chat logs from Conti. [2][SRC-002]

At the time of the leak, a file titled `1.tgz` was posted on the AnonFiles website. Rapid7 reported that it contained:

- 14 megabytes of chat logs
- 393 JSON files [2][SRC-002]

Some messages were encrypted and could not be read. Rapid7 therefore stated that the information was “necessarily incomplete.” [2][SRC-002]

The remaining files contained:

- Internal Conti communications
- Screenshots of tools
- Discussions of exploits
- Discussions of design processes [2][SRC-002]

On February 28 and March 1, additional files were posted, together with a number of pro-Ukraine tweets. [2][SRC-002]

The leaked material included usernames and passwords for various accounts. @ContiLeaks also shared access details for alleged Conti command-and-control servers and storage servers for stolen files. Rapid7 stated that it had not accessed data requiring remote-server access or the use of the credentials and recommended against doing so. [2][SRC-002]

@ContiLeaks also shared a file purporting to be Conti ransomware source code but declined to share the password except with “trusted parties.” [2][SRC-002]

@ContiLeaks named one alleged Conti developer and provided that person’s email address and GitHub account. The returned excerpt does not preserve the developer’s name, email address, or GitHub identifier. [2][SRC-002]

Rapid7 assessed that the scale of the leaked information suggested that the leaker was likely either:

- A very senior member of the group; or
- A coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates. [2][SRC-002]

That statement is an analytical assessment, not a verified identification of the leaker. [2][SRC-002]

## 3.2 Conti as a business

Rapid7’s article includes the heading “Conti is a business – and a well-funded one.” [2][SRC-002]

The article states that much of the discussion within the chat logs concerned “fairly mundane” business matters. The returned excerpt truncates the article after that sentence and does not preserve the further details that followed under that heading. [2][SRC-002]

The available Rapid7 excerpt does preserve the article’s description of the organization as having:

- Sophisticated capability
- Deep funding
- Quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021 [2][SRC-002]

Rapid7 assessed that Conti remained “an active and significant threat” after the chat disclosure because of those characteristics. [2][SRC-002]

## 3.3 Internal political dispute over Russia and Ukraine

Rapid7 stated that, before the chat-log disclosures, Conti pledged support for the Russian government following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. [2][SRC-002]

Rapid7 reported that a number of Conti members sided with Ukraine, causing strife within the organization. [2][SRC-002]

Two days later, Conti posted a second message that revised its earlier statement. According to Rapid7, the revised message condemned the war and stated that Conti would strike back only if Russian critical infrastructure were targeted. [2][SRC-002]

CIS similarly states that, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, Conti operators announced their “full support” for Russia. [3][SRC-003]

CIS states that, “just a few days” after that commitment, the Twitter account called “Contileaks” released an archive of Conti internal chat messages dating back to the beginning of 2021 and also published additional internal chats from 2020. [3][SRC-003]

## 3.4 Business units and employee roles

CIS states that the Conti handlers divided their operations into several business units and recruited staff with specific skill sets. [3][SRC-003]

The article identifies the following internal roles:

- **Coders**, who wrote malicious code and integrated different technologies.
- **Testers**, who validated how the ransomware payload performed against security technologies.
- **Administrators.**
- **Reverse Engineers.**
- **Penetration Testers/Hackers.** [3][SRC-003]

CIS states that spamming functions were contracted outside the organization. [3][SRC-003]

Each department had its own budget, although business units could borrow funds from one another. [3][SRC-003]

According to a Conti insider cited by CIS, the gang employed more than 60 people in July 2021, mostly Coders and Testers. [3][SRC-003]

CIS states that the number of employees did not remain consistent because the group sometimes dismissed people after internal security breaches. [3][SRC-003]

These staffing and organizational details are leak-derived analytical reporting. The returned material does not provide an official organizational chart or a court-verified list of Conti employees. [3][SRC-003]

## 3.5 Product development, testing, and expenditures

CIS states that Conti took steps to improve its “product” on an ongoing basis. [3][SRC-003]

The article identifies the following initiatives:

- Allocating $60,000 to acquire a valid license for the Cobalt Strike network penetration-testing and reconnaissance tool.
- Budgeting several thousand dollars each month for security and antivirus software that Testers could use in their evaluations.
- Redefining the focus of the Reverse Engineers in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11, which was described as Microsoft’s newest operating system at the time. [3][SRC-003]

Rewards for Justice separately lists Cobalt Strike among the malicious cyber applications associated with the Conti/Wizard Spider profile. [1][SRC-001]

The returned material does not establish that any named DOJ defendant purchased, used, developed, or administered Cobalt Strike or any other listed application. [1][SRC-001] [3][SRC-003] [4][SRC-004]

## 3.6 Operational continuity and subsequent dismantling

Rapid7 reported that Conti began taking down exposed infrastructure on March 2, 2022, as a result of the chat disclosure. [2][SRC-002]

Rapid7 nevertheless assessed that Conti remained an active and significant threat because of its sophisticated capability, deep funding, and quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021. [2][SRC-002]

As of March 9, 2022, Rapid7’s threat-intelligence team observed “a resumption of normal operations from Conti.” [2][SRC-002]

CIS states that, in the months following the leaks, Conti handlers began dismantling their operations. [3][SRC-003]

CIS reports that Bleeping Computer wrote in May 2022 that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units. CIS describes the purpose or effect as gaining greater mobility and evading law enforcement. [3][SRC-003]

CIS states that approximately one month later, the RaaS operation shut down its data-leak and negotiation infrastructure. [3][SRC-003]

---

## 4. Law-enforcement alias and defendant links

## 4.1 Aliases officially linked to Conti

Rewards for Justice identifies the following online aliases as belonging to malicious cyber actors “believed to be linked to the Conti ransomware group”:

- “Target”
- “Reshaev”
- “Professor”
- “Tramp”
- “Dandis” [1][SRC-001]

The page gives the associated location as Russia. [1][SRC-001]

It lists Conti and Wizard Spider as the associated cyberthreat organization. [1][SRC-001]

The official wording is “believed to be linked.” The returned source does not state that these aliases are legal names, does not identify the individuals behind them, and does not connect any one of them to Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, or Oleksii Lytvynenko. [1][SRC-001] [4][SRC-004]

## 4.2 Defendants named in the DOJ record

The DOJ page identifies four defendants in case number 3:23-CR-00092:

- Maksim Galochkin
- Maksim Rudenskiy
- Mikhail Tsarev
- Andrey Zhuykov [4][SRC-004]

The DOJ states that, on September 7, 2023, these defendants were charged “for their roles in the Conti ransomware conspiracy.” [4][SRC-004]

The charges were:

- Conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
- Conspiracy to commit wire fraud [4][SRC-004]

The DOJ page identifies Oleksii Lytvynenko in case number 3:23-CR-00088. [4][SRC-004]

The DOJ states that, on November 7, 2025, Lytvynenko was charged “for his role in the Conti ransomware conspiracy” with conspiracy to deploy Conti, “a ransomware variant that infected victim computers and networks, encrypting their data.” [4][SRC-004]

The DOJ page states that Lytvynenko entered a plea of guilty to Count 2 of the indictment, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, on June 10, 2026, pursuant to a plea agreement with the United States. [4][SRC-004]

The page states that Lytvynenko was scheduled to be sentenced on September 10, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. [4][SRC-004]

The DOJ page does not, in the returned excerpt, provide:

- Any online alias for Galochkin
- Any online alias for Rudenskiy
- Any online alias for Tsarev
- Any online alias for Zhuykov
- Any online alias for Lytvynenko
- Any connection between those defendants and “Target”
- Any connection between those defendants and “Reshaev”
- Any connection between those defendants and “Professor”
- Any connection between those defendants and “Tramp”
- Any connection between those defendants and “Dandis” [1][SRC-001] [4][SRC-004]

Accordingly, the benchmark evidence supports two separate official propositions but not an identity crosswalk:

1. Rewards for Justice officially links the five listed aliases collectively to Conti. [1][SRC-001]
2. DOJ officially identifies five people as defendants charged in Conti-related conspiracies, with Lytvynenko later pleading guilty to Count 2. [4][SRC-004]

The returned sources do not establish that any of the five named defendants used any of the five aliases. [1][SRC-001] [4][SRC-004]

## 4.3 Defendant status and procedural posture

The DOJ page expressly states that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. [4][SRC-004]

For Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, and Zhuykov, the returned record shows charges but no conviction or guilty plea. [4][SRC-004]

For Lytvynenko, the page reports a guilty plea to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement. [4][SRC-004]

The returned material does not state the factual basis of Lytvynenko’s plea beyond identifying the count and the Conti-related conspiracy context. [4][SRC-004]

---

## 5. Chronology

### 2019

Rewards for Justice states that Conti ransomware was “first detected in 2019.” [1][SRC-001]

### 2020

CIS states that Contileaks published additional internal Conti chats from 2020. [3][SRC-003]

### Beginning of 2021

CIS states that the first archive of internal communications released by Contileaks included chats dating back to the beginning of 2021. [3][SRC-003]

### July 2021

CIS states that, according to a Conti insider, the gang employed more than 60 people in July 2021, mostly Coders and Testers. [3][SRC-003]

CIS states that Conti redefined the focus of its Reverse Engineers in July 2021 to concentrate on Windows 11. [3][SRC-003]

### November 2021

Rapid7 refers to Conti’s quick recovery from exposed infrastructure in November 2021. [2][SRC-002]

The returned Rapid7 excerpt does not provide further details about the November 2021 infrastructure exposure. [2][SRC-002]

### February 24, 2022

CIS identifies February 24, 2022, as the date of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. [3][SRC-003]

### February 2022

Rewards for Justice states that, after Russian military forces invaded neighboring Ukraine in February 2022, Conti operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to be conducting cyberattacks or war against Russia. [1][SRC-001]

### February 27, 2022

Rapid7 states that Twitter user @ContiLeaks released a trove of Conti chat logs on February 27, 2022. [2][SRC-002]

CIS states that, a few days after Conti announced “full support” for Russia, Contileaks dumped an archive of internal chats. [3][SRC-003]

### February 28 and March 1, 2022

Rapid7 states that additional files were posted on February 28 and March 1, together with pro-Ukraine tweets. [2][SRC-002]

### March 1, 2022

Rapid7’s article is dated March 1, 2022. [2][SRC-002]

### March 2, 2022

Rapid7 states that Conti began taking down exposed infrastructure on March 2 as a result of the chat disclosure. [2][SRC-002]

### March 9, 2022

Rapid7 states that its threat-intelligence team observed a resumption of normal operations from Conti as of March 9, 2022. [2][SRC-002]

### May 2022

CIS states that Bleeping Computer reported in May 2022 that the larger Conti platform had shut down and rebranded into several smaller units. [3][SRC-003]

### Approximately June 2022

CIS states that approximately one month after the reported May 2022 shutdown and rebranding, the RaaS operation shut down its data-leak and negotiation infrastructure. [3][SRC-003]

### September 7, 2023

The DOJ states that Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, and Zhuykov were charged on September 7, 2023, with conspiracy to violate the CFAA and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. [4][SRC-004]

### November 7, 2025

The DOJ states that Oleksii Lytvynenko was charged on November 7, 2025, with conspiracy to deploy Conti. [4][SRC-004]

### June 10, 2026

The DOJ states that Lytvynenko pleaded guilty to Count 2 of the indictment, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, pursuant to a plea agreement. [4][SRC-004]

### September 10, 2026

The DOJ page lists Lytvynenko’s sentencing for September 10, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. [4][SRC-004]

### July 8, 2026

The DOJ page states that it was updated July 8, 2026. [4][SRC-004]

---

## 6. Verified facts versus alleged, reported, or assessed claims

## 6.1 Officially recorded facts

The following are directly stated in official government sources:

- Rewards for Justice offers a reward of up to $10 million for information concerning malicious cyber actors involved in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure under the circumstances described on the page. [1][SRC-001]
- Rewards for Justice identifies “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis” as aliases of actors believed to be linked to Conti. [1][SRC-001]
- Rewards for Justice identifies Conti as also known as Wizard Spider. [1][SRC-001]
- Rewards for Justice describes Conti as a Russian government-linked RaaS group. [1][SRC-001]
- Rewards for Justice states that Conti was first detected in 2019. [1][SRC-001]
- Rewards for Justice states that Conti ransomware was used in more than 1,000 ransomware operations and that more than 400 organizations worldwide, including over 290 in the United States, were victimized. [1][SRC-001]
- The DOJ lists Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, and Zhuykov as defendants in case 3:23-CR-00092. [4][SRC-004]
- The DOJ lists Lytvynenko as a defendant in case 3:23-CR-00088. [4][SRC-004]
- The DOJ states that the four defendants in case 3:23-CR-00092 were charged with conspiracy to violate the CFAA and conspiracy to commit wire fraud. [4][SRC-004]
- The DOJ states that Lytvynenko was charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti. [4][SRC-004]
- The DOJ states that Lytvynenko pleaded guilty to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud. [4][SRC-004]
- The DOJ expressly states that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. [4][SRC-004]

## 6.2 Allegations or qualified official claims

The following language is qualified or allegation-based in the official source:

- The five aliases are “believed to be linked” to Conti; the official page does not present a completed identity determination for the people behind the aliases. [1][SRC-001]
- Rewards for Justice describes Conti as Russian government-linked. The returned excerpt does not provide the underlying evidentiary basis for that characterization. [1][SRC-001]
- The DOJ’s charging statements concerning Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, Zhuykov, and Lytvynenko are charges and accusations in criminal proceedings. The DOJ page states that the defendants are presumed innocent. [4][SRC-004]
- Rapid7 refers to alleged Conti command-and-control servers and alleged stolen-file storage servers. [2][SRC-002]
- Rapid7 refers to a file that @ContiLeaks purported to be Conti ransomware source code. [2][SRC-002]
- Rapid7 refers to one alleged Conti developer identified by @ContiLeaks. [2][SRC-002]
- Rapid7 assesses that the leaker was likely either a very senior group member or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates. [2][SRC-002]
- CIS states that Conti “appears to have had ties” to other malware groups, most notably TrickBot. [3][SRC-003]
- CIS’s descriptions of internal business units, employee roles, staffing levels, budgets, and product-development initiatives are based on analyses of leaks and reporting about those leaks, not on an official Conti organizational chart or a judicial finding in the returned materials. [3][SRC-003]

## 6.3 Analytical assessments and media reporting

The following claims are analytical or reported rather than directly established as official adjudicated facts in the returned sources:

- Rapid7’s assessment that Conti remained an active and significant threat because of its sophisticated capability, deep funding, and recovery from exposed infrastructure. [2][SRC-002]
- Rapid7’s assessment that Conti resumed normal operations as of March 9, 2022, based on its threat-intelligence observations. [2][SRC-002]
- CIS’s account that the larger Conti platform shut down, rebranded into smaller units, and later shut down its leak and negotiation infrastructure. CIS attributes the May 2022 shutdown and rebranding to Bleeping Computer reporting. [3][SRC-003]
- CIS’s statement that the Conti leaks provided insight into how a major RaaS group ran its “office” and improved its “product.” [3][SRC-003]
- CIS’s account of departments, employee roles, external spamming contractors, department budgets, staffing levels, employee dismissals, Cobalt Strike expenditures, security-software budgets, and Windows 11 testing. [3][SRC-003]
- Rapid7’s description of the leak archive, unreadable encrypted messages, exposed credentials, alleged server access, and purported ransomware source code. [2][SRC-002]

---

## 7. Contradictions, differences, and unresolved uncertainties

## 7.1 Number of operations versus number of affected organizations

Rewards for Justice states that Conti ransomware was used in “more than 1,000 ransomware operations” and that more than 400 organizations worldwide, including over 290 in the United States, were victimized. [1][SRC-001]

The DOJ states that Conti ransomware affected “more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims” in the United States and around the world. [4][SRC-004]

These figures are not directly equivalent:

- “More than 1,000 ransomware operations” refers to operations.
- “More than 400 organizations worldwide” refers to organizations identified in the Rewards for Justice description.
- “More than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims” refers to victims in the DOJ case-page description. [1][SRC-001] [4][SRC-004]

The returned sources do not explain the difference between the figures or establish whether they use the same time period, counting method, or victim definition.

## 7.2 Leak disclosure and operational continuity

Rapid7 states that Conti took down exposed infrastructure on March 2, 2022, but observed a resumption of normal operations by March 9, 2022. [2][SRC-002]

CIS states that Conti’s handlers began dismantling operations in the months following the leaks, that the larger platform shut down and rebranded into smaller units in May 2022, and that the RaaS operation later shut down its data-leak and negotiation infrastructure. [3][SRC-003]

These statements can describe different stages or components of the operation, but the returned sources do not fully reconcile:

- Rapid7’s “resumption of normal operations” in March 2022;
- CIS’s later account of shutdown and rebranding in May 2022; and
- CIS’s later account of the shutdown of data-leak and negotiation infrastructure. [2][SRC-002] [3][SRC-003]

The sources do not establish whether “normal operations” referred to the whole organization, particular infrastructure, or only observed activity during that period.

## 7.3 Different descriptions of the Russia-related statements

Rapid7 states that Conti initially pledged support for the Russian government, that members sided with Ukraine, and that two days later Conti revised its statement to condemn the war and threaten retaliation only if Russian critical infrastructure were targeted. [2][SRC-002]

CIS states that Conti announced its “full support” for Russia after the February 24, 2022 invasion and that Contileaks released the chats a few days later. [3][SRC-003]

Rewards for Justice states that Conti operators pledged support to the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure organizations of countries perceived to be conducting cyberattacks or war against the Russian government. [1][SRC-001]

The returned sources do not reproduce the full original or revised Conti statements, and they do not provide a source-based resolution of whether the revised message represented a change in organizational policy, a public-relations position, or a division within the group.

## 7.4 Alias-to-defendant uncertainty

Rewards for Justice provides five aliases linked collectively to Conti:

- Target
- Reshaev
- Professor
- Tramp
- Dandis [1][SRC-001]

The DOJ provides five named defendants linked to Conti-related criminal cases:

- Maksim Galochkin
- Maksim Rudenskiy
- Mikhail Tsarev
- Andrey Zhuykov
- Oleksii Lytvynenko [4][SRC-004]

No returned source maps any alias to any named defendant. [1][SRC-001] [4][SRC-004]

The evidence therefore does not support:

- Treating the five aliases as aliases of the five defendants;
- Assigning one alias to one defendant;
- Treating the aliases and defendants as the same set of people;
- Inferring that every person behind a listed alias was charged in the DOJ cases; or
- Inferring that every DOJ defendant used one of the listed aliases. [1][SRC-001] [4][SRC-004]

## 7.5 Conti, Wizard Spider, and related malware

Rewards for Justice expressly states that Conti is “also known as Wizard Spider.” [1][SRC-001]

The same page lists TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader as associated malicious cyber applications. [1][SRC-001]

CIS says that Conti “appears to have had ties” to other malware outfits, “most notably TrickBot.” [3][SRC-003]

The returned sources do not specify:

- Whether Wizard Spider was an organization, an alias, a broader criminal ecosystem, or a label used in a particular attribution framework;
- Whether TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader were controlled by the same people as Conti;
- Which individuals, if any, were responsible for those applications;
- Whether any named DOJ defendant was involved with those applications. [1][SRC-001] [3][SRC-003] [4][SRC-004]

## 7.6 Incomplete leak evidence

Rapid7 states that some messages were encrypted and unreadable, making the information necessarily incomplete. [2][SRC-002]

Rapid7 also states that it did not access the alleged remote servers or use the leaked credentials. [2][SRC-002]

Accordingly, the returned leak analysis cannot establish the complete Conti organizational structure, all personnel identities, all internal roles, all infrastructure, or all operational relationships. [2][SRC-002]

## 7.7 Missing official documents

The searches specifically sought official indictments, complaints, warrants, sanctions, advisories, and alias links. The returned benchmark results did not include additional documents beyond the four sources listed above.

The DOJ result is a case summary page and not the full indictment, complaint, warrant, or press release. [4][SRC-004]

The returned evidence therefore does not provide:

- The factual allegations in the indictments;
- The alleged conduct attributed to each named defendant;
- The dates or locations of each defendant’s alleged activity;
- The aliases allegedly used by each defendant;
- The technical or financial evidence underlying the charges;
- Any warrant application or affidavit;
- Any sanctions designation;
- Any FBI or CISA advisory text;
- Any court findings beyond the reported Lytvynenko guilty plea. [4][SRC-004]
